title: Motion Along a Straight Line
learning_objectives: Describe one dimensional motion in terms of position, displacement, distance, velocity, speed and acceleration.
Tell a scalar from a vector and apply that distinction to the quantities of motion.
Use the equations of constant acceleration to solve problems about motion in a straight line.
Read a motion from a position time graph and from a velocity time graph.

sections.title: Introduction to One-Dimensional Kinematics
objectives: Describe what kinematics studies and how it differs from dynamics.

misconceptions.claim: Kinematics and dynamics are two names for the same subject.
misconceptions.correction: Kinematics describes how things move, with no mention of a cause. Dynamics explains why they move, through forces.

summary: Kinematics describes motion in terms of position and time.
One dimensional motion happens along a straight line.
Kinematics comes first, because the causes of motion come later.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Displacement
objectives: Define position and displacement on a coordinate system, and tell displacement from distance.
Use the sign of displacement to state its direction on a chosen axis.

misconceptions.claim: Distance and displacement are the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Distance is the length of the path and is never negative. Displacement is the straight line from the start to the end, and it carries a direction.

misconceptions.claim: Distance travelled and displacement are the same quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Distance is the length of the path, 10 m here. Displacement is the change in position, 2 m east.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-1, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the distance as an option.

summary: Position locates an object on a coordinate system.
Displacement is the change in position, and it is a vector.
Distance is the total path length, and it is a scalar.

sections.title: Vectors, Scalars, and Coordinate Systems
objectives: Tell a scalar from a vector, and place a point on a one dimensional coordinate system.
Use a number line with an origin and a positive direction to assign signs to position and displacement.

misconceptions.claim: Speed and velocity mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is a scalar, the distance over time. Velocity is a vector, the displacement over time, and it also carries a direction.

summary: A scalar has magnitude only. A vector has magnitude and direction.
Displacement and velocity are vectors. Distance and speed are scalars.
A one dimensional coordinate system is a number line with an origin and a positive direction.

authored_exercises.stem: Which of these is a vector: distance, displacement, speed or time? Explain your choice.
authored_exercises.answer: Displacement is the vector. It has magnitude and direction; the other three have magnitude only.
solution: A vector must have both magnitude and direction.
Displacement is the change in position, so it carries a direction.
Distance, speed and time are scalars: they have magnitude only.

authored_exercises.stem: A point lies 4 m to the left of the origin on a number line. Taking right as positive, what is its coordinate?
solution: The origin is 0 and the positive direction is to the right.
A point 4 m to the left has coordinate -4 m.

authored_exercises.stem: A student walks 3 m east and then 4 m west. Taking east as positive, find the distance travelled and the displacement.
solution: Distance is the total path length: 3 m + 4 m = 7 m.
Displacement is final position minus initial position: 3 m - 4 m = -1 m.
The negative sign means the displacement points west.

authored_exercises.stem: What does the sign of a position tell you on a one-dimensional coordinate system?
authored_exercises.answer: It tells you which side of the origin the point lies on, given the chosen positive direction.
solution: Choose an origin and a positive direction.
A positive coordinate is on the positive side of the origin.
A negative coordinate is on the opposite side.

sections.title: Time, Velocity, and Speed
objectives: Define average velocity and average speed, and compute them from a motion diagram.
Distinguish average speed, average velocity and instantaneous speed.

misconceptions.claim: Average velocity tells you how fast the object is moving right now.
misconceptions.correction: Average velocity covers the whole journey. The speed at a moment is the instantaneous speed.

misconceptions.claim: Average velocity tells you how fast an object is moving at this moment.
misconceptions.correction: It covers the whole journey. The speed at a moment is the instantaneous speed.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-2, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the instantaneous reading as an option.

summary: Average velocity is displacement over time.
Average speed is distance over time.
Average speed is never smaller than the magnitude of the average velocity.

sections.title: Acceleration
objectives: Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity and read it from a velocity time graph.
Compute acceleration from a change in velocity and interpret its sign.

misconceptions.claim: An object with zero acceleration must be at rest.
misconceptions.correction: Zero acceleration means the velocity is not changing. The object may be moving at a constant velocity.

summary: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so it is a vector.
Positive acceleration means the velocity is increasing, negative means it is decreasing.
The sign of acceleration does not tell you the direction of the motion.

sections.title: Motion Equations for Constant Acceleration in One Dimension
objectives: Use the equations of constant acceleration, and choose which one fits the question.
Solve for any one of displacement, velocity, acceleration or time when the other three are known.

misconceptions.claim: The constant acceleration equations work for any motion.
misconceptions.correction: They hold only while the acceleration stays constant. If the acceleration changes, the equations do not apply.

misconceptions.claim: The equations of constant acceleration hold for any motion.
misconceptions.correction: They hold only while the acceleration stays constant.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the answer for a changing acceleration as an option.

summary: The equations relate position, velocity, acceleration and time for constant acceleration.
Each equation leaves out one of the quantities.
Choose the equation by listing what you know and what you want.

sections.title: Problem-Solving Basics for One-Dimensional Kinematics
objectives: Set up a kinematics problem: draw it, list what is known, choose the equation, solve, and check.
Apply one sign convention consistently and check that an answer is physically reasonable.

misconceptions.claim: You can start algebra on a physics problem without knowing which quantities you have.
misconceptions.correction: List what is known and what is wanted first. Then the equation chooses itself.

summary: Draw the situation, then list what is known and what is wanted.
Choose the equation, solve, and check the signs and the units.
A sign convention applies to every quantity, not only to the answer.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section, and it holds no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

authored_exercises.stem: List the first three steps in solving a one-dimensional kinematics problem.
authored_exercises.answer: Draw the situation, list the known and unknown quantities, then choose an equation that connects them.
solution: Draw a sketch and mark the positive direction.
List the knowns and the quantity you want.
Choose the equation that contains those quantities and no others.

authored_exercises.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Find its final velocity.
solution: List the knowns: u = 0, a = 2 m/s², t = 5 s.
The equation without displacement is v = u + at.

authored_exercises.stem: A train slows from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over a distance of 200 m. Find its acceleration.
solution: List the knowns: u = 30 m/s, v = 10 m/s, s = 200 m.
The equation without time is v² = u² + 2as.
The negative sign means the acceleration opposes the motion.

sections.title: Falling Objects
objectives: Model free fall as constant acceleration and read the motion off a motion diagram.
Explain why air resistance makes a real fall depart from free fall.

misconceptions.claim: A heavier object falls faster than a lighter one.
misconceptions.correction: Without air resistance every object falls with the same acceleration, whatever its mass. Air resistance is what separates a feather from a stone.

summary: Near the Earth's surface, free fall has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s² downward.
The acceleration is the same for every object. The velocity is not.
Air resistance makes real falls differ from the model.

sections.title: Graphical Analysis of One-Dimensional Motion
objectives: Read a position time graph and a velocity time graph, and use their slopes and areas.
Relate the area under a velocity-time graph to displacement and the area under an acceleration-time graph to velocity.

misconceptions.claim: The area under a velocity time graph is the distance travelled.
misconceptions.correction: The area under the curve is the displacement, because velocity is signed. Distance is the area under the speed curve, where the speed is never negative.

summary: The slope of a position time graph is the velocity.
The slope of a velocity time graph is the acceleration.
The area under a velocity time graph is the displacement.

authored_exercises.stem: A cyclist rides along a straight road at a constant 6.0 m/s for 40 s, then slows uniformly to rest over the next 20 s. (a) Sketch the velocity-time graph for the ride. (b) Use the area under the graph to find the total distance travelled. (c) Use the slope of the graph to find the cyclist's acceleration during the final 20 s.
authored_exercises.answer: (a) A horizontal line at 6.0 m/s from t = 0 to 40 s, then a straight line falling to zero at t = 60 s. (b) The area is the rectangle 6.0 × 40 = 240 m plus the triangle ½ × 6.0 × 20 = 60 m, so the distance is 300 m. (c) The slope is (0 - 6.0)/20 = -0.30 m/s².
solution: From t = 0 to 40 s the velocity is constant at 6.0 m/s; from t = 40 s to 60 s it falls uniformly to 0.
Distance = area under the graph = 6.0 × 40 + ½ × 6.0 × 20 = 240 + 60 = 300 m.
Acceleration = slope = (0 - 6.0)/20 = -0.30 m/s².

definition.text: The study of how objects move, without asking what causes the motion.
The location of an object on a coordinate system, measured from the origin.
The change in position of an object, with direction. It is the straight line from the start to the end, not the path.
Displacement divided by the time it took, so it is a vector.
The rate at which the velocity changes with time. It is a vector.

sec-2:exr-39.stem: An object moves along the $x$-axis from $x=0\ \mathrm{m}$ to $x=7.0\ \mathrm{m}$. (a) What distance does it travel? (b) What is the magnitude of its displacement? (c) What is its displacement?
solution: (a) The path is 7.0 m long, so the distance traveled is $7\ \mathrm{m}$.
(b) The displacement is $\Delta x=7.0-0=+7.0\ \mathrm{m}$, so its magnitude is $7\ \mathrm{m}$.
(c) The displacement is $+7\ \mathrm{m}$, with the positive direction along the $x$-axis.

sec-2:exr-43.stem: An object starts at $x=2.0\ \mathrm{m}$, moves to $x=10.0\ \mathrm{m}$, then back to $x=8.0\ \mathrm{m}$, and finally to $x=11.0\ \mathrm{m}$. (a) What distance does it travel? (b) What is the magnitude of its displacement? (c) What is its displacement?
solution: (a) Add the lengths of the three legs: $8\ \mathrm{m}+2\ \mathrm{m}+3\ \mathrm{m}=13\ \mathrm{m}$.
(b) The displacement is final position minus initial position: $11\ \mathrm{m}-2\ \mathrm{m}=+9\ \mathrm{m}$, so its magnitude is $9\ \mathrm{m}$.
(c) The displacement is $+9\ \mathrm{m}$, in the positive $x$-direction.

sec-9:exr-84.stem: An object moves along a straight line. Its position was measured at the times shown: $t=0,\ 10.0,\ 20.0,\ 30.0,\ 40.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and $x=0,\ 2.1,\ 4.4,\ 6.9,\ 9.6\ \mathrm{m}$. (a) Estimate the slope of the position-time graph at $t=10.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and at $t=30.0\ \mathrm{s}$ to find the velocity at those times. (b) Use your answers to estimate the acceleration at $t=20\ \mathrm{s}$. Assume all values are known to two significant figures.
solution: (a) Use a central difference around $t=10.0\ \mathrm{s}$: $v\approx(x_{20}-x_{0})/(20.0-0)=(4.4-0)/20.0=0.22\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
(b) The acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time: $a\approx(0.26-0.22)/(30.0-10.0)=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s^{2}}$.
